title: Correcting in Hindsight: Editing Past Key-Value States for Robust LLM Reasoning
claim: Standard decoding commits early errors and cannot revise them; ours detects inconsistency, edits the past, and reaches the correct outcome.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left-to-right contrast, path-metaphor cartoon above worked text example
description: Two panels split by a dotted vertical line. Panel (a), titled 'Base model', shows a cartoon forked road. A stick figure walks down a red path toward a dark cloud marked with a red X, and a second figure looks puzzled under a blue question mark. Panel (b), titled 'Ours', shows the same fork. A dashed arrow with a red wrench sends the figure back to the fork. A green path then leads to a flag with a green check. Below each cartoon is a math query (x + y = 10, can it equal 45?) and a short answer. In (a) the wrong value '2' is boxed in red and 'contradicts' in blue, ending in a red X badge. In (b) the corrected '3' is boxed in green and 'consistent' in green, ending in a green check badge. The eye goes first to the red and green paths.
caption: Autoregressive reasoning failures and our solution. (a) In standard autoregressive decoding, an early error at a critical anchor token (red) is silently propagated until it manifests as uncertainty or contradiction at a later trigger point (blue), where the model cannot revise its past reasoning. (b) Our method detects such trigger points, locates the responsible anchor token, retroactively edits its key-value states, and resumes reasoning along a corrected trajectory.
abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail in complex reasoning because early-stage errors remain uncorrectable in subsequent steps—a limitation fundamentally rooted in the inherent irreversibility of the Transformer architecture. In this paper, we propose HEdit, a lightweight reasoning enhancement paradigm that equips models with a "hindsight-like" capability for dynamic error correction during generation. Our core insight involves deconstructing reasoning failures into two pivotal stages: latent representational biases emerging at logical anchors, and the subsequent eruption of explicit cognitive dissonance at trigger points. Based on these observations, the HEdit framework detects internal inconsistency signals at trigger points in real-time, actively backtracks to critical anchors, and utilizes a lightweight trainable editor to precisely refine their Key-Value (KV) caches. This mechanism effectively breaks the unidirectional constraints of autoregressive inference. Empirical results demonstrate that HEdit significantly enhances the performance of various models on mathematical reasoning tasks—with average accuracy improvements ranging from 2.2\% to 10.8\%—while maintaining extremely low overhead (add parameters $<0.5\%$). HEdit provides a dynamic, pluggable and lightweight solution, making it particularly beneficial for users in low-resource environments.
